content: Rigor, also referred to as shaking chills or shivering, describes a sensation of coldness that can occur after exposure to a cold environment. It may also refer to episodes of shivering accompanied by paleness and a feeling of being cold. Overview of Rigor Chills are often associated with the body's response to feeling cold. Goosebumps, which raise the hairs on the body to create a layer of insulation, may occur with a sensation of chilliness but are not always linked to chills or fevers. Chills are typically caused by rapid muscle contractions and relaxations, which generate heat when the body perceives itself as cold. They often precede the onset of a fever or an increase in the body's core temperature. In some diseases, such as malaria, chills can be a significant and consistent clinical finding. Chills are more common in young children, who tend to develop higher fevers than adults, even with minor illnesses. Infants, however, may not exhibit obvious chills, but any fever in an infant under six months of age should be reported to a healthcare provider. Similarly, fevers in infants aged six months to one year should be reported unless the cause is absolutely certain. Causes of Rigor Rigor can result from various conditions, including: Exposure to a cold environment Viral and bacterial infections, such as: Bacterial gastroenteritis Common colds Infectious mononucleosis Influenza Meningitis Pneumonia Strep throat Viral gastroenteritis Urinary tract infections, including pyelonephritis Diagnosis A healthcare provider will take a detailed medical history and perform a physical examination. Questions may include: Is it just a sensation of cold, or are you actually shaking? What has been the highest body temperature associated with the chills? Did the chills occur only once, or are they episodic? How long does each episode last? Did the chills occur within 4–6 hours of exposure to an allergen? Did they start suddenly or occur repeatedly? If so, how often? What other symptoms are present? The physical examination will likely focus on the skin, eyes, ears, nose, throat, neck, chest, and abdomen. Body temperature will also be checked. Diagnostic tests may include: Blood tests (e.g., CBC or blood differential) and urine tests (e.g., urinalysis) Blood culture Sputum culture Urine culture Chest X-ray When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Seek immediate medical attention if: There is neck stiffness, confusion, significant irritability, or sluggishness. There is a significant cough, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, burning sensation, or frequent urination. A child younger than three months has a temperature of 101°F (38.3°C) or higher. A child between three months and one year has a fever lasting more than 24 hours. The fever remains above 103°F (39.4°C) after 1–2 hours of home treatment. The fever does not improve after three days or lasts more than five days. Treatment Options Treatment depends on the duration of the chills and accompanying symptoms, particularly fever. Home Care for Fever Fever, which often accompanies chills, is the body's natural response to various conditions, such as infections. If the fever is mild (102°F or less) and there are no side effects, professional treatment is not required. Drink plenty of fluids and get adequate rest. Evaporation cools the skin and reduces body temperature. Sponging with comfortably warm water (around 70°F) may help reduce fever. Avoid cold water, as it can be uncomfortable and may increase fever by triggering chills. Medications like acetaminophen are effective for managing fever and chills. Avoid bundling up in blankets if you have a high temperature, as this can cause the fever to rise. Home Care for a Child If a child's temperature exceeds 102°F or if the child is uncomfortable, administer pain-relieving medications such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Follow the recommended dosage on the package label. Avoid giving aspirin to children with viral infection symptoms due to the risk of Reye syndrome. After 1–2 hours of administering fever medication, place the child in a tub of lukewarm water up to the navel. Use a wet washcloth or towel to gently rub the child's body for 20 minutes or as long as tolerated. Add warm water as needed to maintain a constant water temperature and prevent shivering. Pat the child dry with a towel (do not rub). Dress the child in light clothing, provide fluids, and keep the room cool but comfortable. Avoid using ice water or rubbing alcohol to reduce a child's temperature, as these can cause shock. Do not bundle a feverish child in blankets. Do not wake a sleeping child to administer medication or take their temperature—rest is more important.
